stem: A marketing team is setting up a brand-voice Project. They have a 30-page brand guidelines PDF and a short rule: "Always write in British English and never use exclamation marks." Where should each go?

options.text: Paste the whole PDF and the rule into the project instructions.
options.why: Thirty pages of reference material bloats the instructions and buries the rule; long instructions are harder for Claude to follow consistently.

options.text: Upload the PDF as project knowledge and put the rule in the project instructions.
options.why: Knowledge holds reference material Claude draws on; instructions hold the short, always-on rules about role, tone, format and constraints.

options.text: Upload both the PDF and a text file containing the rule as project knowledge.
options.why: A rule buried in a knowledge file is reference material, not a standing instruction; it may not be applied on every request.

options.text: Leave the Project empty and repeat the rule and key guideline points in every prompt.
options.why: Repeating context in every prompt is what Projects exist to avoid; it is error-prone and inconsistent across team members.

explanation: Project instructions are for concise, standing guidance (role, tone, format, constraints); project knowledge is for the documents Claude should reference. Keeping the two separate keeps instructions short and the material available.
reference: Claude Help Center — How can I create and manage projects?

stem: An HR lead built an onboarding Project by pasting nine pages of the employee handbook into the project instructions, followed by a paragraph describing Claude's role and a friendly tone. Claude's answers are accurate on policy but often ignore the tone guidance and the requested format. What change is most likely to fix this?

options.text: Repeat the tone and format guidance three times at different points in the instructions, so Claude encounters it before, during and after the handbook text.
options.why: Repetition inside an overloaded instruction block does not address the cause, which is that the instructions are mostly reference text.

options.text: Move everything, including the role and tone guidance, into a single knowledge file.
options.why: Standing guidance about role and tone belongs in instructions; as a knowledge file it becomes reference material that may not shape every answer.

options.text: Create a separate Project for each chapter of the handbook.
options.why: Splitting by chapter multiplies maintenance and forces users to guess which Project to use; the handbook belongs together as knowledge.

options.text: Move the handbook into project knowledge and cut the instructions to a short statement of role, tone, format and constraints.
options.why: The help centre advice is to keep instructions concise and focused on general context, key guidelines and Claude's role; the handbook is reference material and belongs in knowledge.

explanation: Overloaded instructions dilute the guidance that matters. Put reference documents in knowledge, and keep instructions short and specific about role, tone, format and constraints.
reference: Claude Help Center — Understanding Claude's personalization features; How can I create and manage projects?

stem: A consultant is configuring a Project for a new client engagement with a logistics company. Which two configuration choices are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: Upload the client's raw customer database export as knowledge so Claude has full context.
options.why: A customer database contains personal data the engagement does not need in Claude; it breaches data-minimisation and likely the client's policy.

options.text: Add the discovery notes, statement of work and org chart as knowledge files with descriptive names such as `sow-2026-03.pdf`.
options.why: These are the reference documents the work depends on, and descriptive filenames help Claude and the team find and cite the right source.

options.text: Write the instructions as "Be helpful, accurate and professional."
options.why: Generic adjectives give Claude nothing specific to follow; effective instructions name the role, outputs and constraints.

options.text: Write instructions that define Claude's role as engagement analyst, the format for deliverables, and what to do when information is missing (ask rather than assume).
options.why: Role, format and a rule for missing information are the specific, always-on guidance that makes outputs consistent and keeps Claude from inventing client facts.

options.text: Skip instructions entirely, since the knowledge files provide all the context Claude needs.
options.why: Knowledge tells Claude what the facts are, not how to behave; without instructions, tone, format and handling of gaps vary from chat to chat.

explanation: Configure a Project with the relevant reference material as clearly named knowledge files and concise instructions covering role, output format and how to handle gaps. Keep unnecessary personal data out and avoid vague adjectives.
reference: Claude Help Center — How can I create and manage projects?; Retrieval augmented generation (RAG) for projects (descriptive filenames)

stem: An operations team on a Team plan needs a shared vendor-triage Project for six people. Two of them should be able to change the instructions and knowledge; the other four only need to use it. The vendor contracts live in a Google Drive folder, but when the team tries to add them from Drive to the shared Project, the Google Drive option is disabled. Which setup meets the team's needs?

options.text: Share the Project with "Can edit" for the two maintainers and "Can view" for the other four, upload the contract files directly as project knowledge, and agree a routine for replacing them when contracts change.
options.why: The two permission levels match the roles exactly, uploaded knowledge works in a shared Project, and a refresh routine covers what Drive syncing would have done.

options.text: Give all six people "Can edit" so anyone can add files whenever the option becomes available.
options.why: Editing rights for everyone invites uncoordinated changes to instructions and knowledge, which is the main cause of drifting shared Projects.

options.text: Have each of the six people create a private copy of the Project so they can each add the Drive files.
options.why: Six private copies will diverge immediately and lose the single shared configuration the team wanted.

options.text: Make the Project visible to the whole organisation instead of sharing it with the six people.
options.why: Organisation-wide visibility changes who can see the Project, not whether Drive files can be added to a shared one, and exposes vendor contracts more widely than needed.

explanation: On Team and Enterprise plans, share Projects with the narrowest permission that fits each role (view versus edit). The help centre notes that Google Drive files can be added only to private Projects, so a shared Project uses uploaded knowledge and a maintenance routine instead.
reference: Claude Help Center — Manage project visibility and sharing; Use Google Workspace connectors (adding Drive files to projects)

stem: A product manager's requirements Project holds about 60 specification documents, and the Project has automatically switched to retrieval (RAG) mode because the knowledge exceeds the context window. The team keeps a one-page glossary that must be applied to every answer (for example, "customer" always means the paying account, not the end user), but Claude now applies the glossary inconsistently. The large specifications are still needed. Which change best fixes the problem?

options.text: Remove most of the specifications so the Project drops back below the context limit and retrieval mode turns off, then re-add documents one at a time as needed.
options.why: The specifications are needed; removing them sacrifices the Project's purpose to work around the glossary problem.

options.text: Add "Always read the glossary first" to every prompt.
options.why: Per-prompt reminders depend on each user remembering and still rely on retrieval fetching the glossary file.

options.text: Move the glossary into the project instructions, which apply to every chat, and keep the specifications in knowledge.
options.why: Instructions apply to every conversation in the Project, whereas knowledge in retrieval mode is fetched by relevance; a short, always-needed glossary belongs in instructions.

options.text: Split the specifications across ten smaller Projects so each stays under the context limit.
options.why: Fragmenting the knowledge makes cross-document questions impossible and multiplies the glossary problem across ten configurations.

explanation: When project knowledge is large enough for retrieval mode, Claude fetches knowledge by relevance rather than loading all of it. Short guidance that must apply to every answer belongs in project instructions; bulky reference material stays in knowledge.
reference: Claude Help Center — Retrieval augmented generation (RAG) for projects; What are projects?

stem: A member of an operations team on a Team plan wants Claude to search the shared vendor inbox through the Gmail connector, but cannot find a way to turn it on in her account. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Gmail can only be reached by building a custom remote MCP connector.
options.why: Gmail is a standard Google Workspace connector in the connectors directory; no custom build is needed.

options.text: Emails have to be exported from Gmail and uploaded as project knowledge before Claude can read them, because connectors cannot reach mailboxes directly.
options.why: Uploading exports is a workaround, not a requirement; the connector exists to search live mail.

options.text: An Owner has to enable the connector for the organisation first, after which each member authenticates individually.
options.why: This is how connectors work for organisations: admin enablement at the org level, then per-person authentication.

options.text: The Gmail connector is only available on individual Pro and Max plans.
options.why: Google Workspace connectors are available on Team and Enterprise plans once enabled by an Owner.

explanation: Connectors on Team and Enterprise plans are enabled by an Owner or Primary Owner for the organisation, after which each member connects their own account. Enablement does not grant access; authentication is individual.
reference: Claude Help Center — Use connectors to extend Claude's capabilities; Use Google Workspace connectors

stem: A marketing manager has connected Google Drive and asks Claude to summarise the "Q3 brand review" document that a colleague created. Claude reports that it cannot find the document. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The document has not been shared with her in Drive, and Claude can only reach files she can already access.
options.why: Connectors mirror the user's own permissions in the source system; a file she cannot open in Drive is invisible to Claude too.

options.text: The Google Drive connector only reads files that Claude itself created or that were saved to Drive from a Claude conversation.
options.why: The connector searches and retrieves the user's accessible Drive files, not only Claude-generated ones.

options.text: Documents must be uploaded to a Project before a connector can read them.
options.why: Connectors read live from the source; uploading to a Project is a separate way of providing knowledge.

options.text: The document is too long for Claude to retrieve.
options.why: Length limits would produce a different failure (truncation or a size message), not an inability to find the file.

explanation: Claude inherits each person's permissions from the connected service. If someone cannot access a file, channel or record in the source system, the connector cannot reach it from Claude either.
reference: Claude Help Center — Use connectors to extend Claude's capabilities (permission inheritance)

stem: An HR team maintains an onboarding Project whose knowledge includes the benefits policy, the leave policy and several Google Docs added from Drive. Which two statements about managing this knowledge are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: Google Docs added to a private Project from Drive sync with the source, so Claude works from the latest version.
options.why: Synced Google Docs stay current automatically, which is one reason to add them from Drive rather than as static copies.

options.text: A PDF uploaded as knowledge updates automatically whenever the original on the shared drive changes.
options.why: An uploaded file is a static copy; it has no link to the original and must be replaced by hand when the policy changes.

options.text: When a policy is replaced, remove the superseded file rather than adding the new version alongside it.
options.why: Two versions of the same policy in knowledge make it a coin toss which one Claude cites; removing the old one keeps answers consistent.

options.text: Keeping all historical versions of each policy in knowledge helps Claude reconcile differences.
options.why: Conflicting versions produce inconsistent, sometimes outdated answers; Claude does not know which version is authoritative unless only the current one is present.

options.text: Retrieval (RAG) mode has to be switched on manually once the knowledge approaches the context limit.
options.why: Retrieval mode activates automatically on paid plans when knowledge approaches or exceeds the limit; no configuration is required.

explanation: Manage knowledge deliberately: use Drive-synced Google Docs where live currency matters, replace static uploads when their source changes, and remove superseded versions so only the authoritative document remains. Retrieval mode is automatic.
reference: Claude Help Center — Use Google Workspace connectors; Retrieval augmented generation (RAG) for projects

stem: A consultant on a Pro plan needs live data from a client's ticketing system. The client's IT team offers a remote MCP server as a custom connector. The consultant is concerned that the server has not been verified by Anthropic, that content returned by its tools could carry prompt-injection attempts, and that the connector can take actions in the ticketing system. Which approach manages these risks while still getting the data?

options.text: Decline all custom connectors and ask the client to email ticket exports each week instead.
options.why: Refusing outright discards the live data the engagement needs; the risks can be managed rather than avoided.

options.text: Confirm the server comes from the client's own trusted organisation, authenticate with OAuth rather than sharing a password, enable the connector only in conversations that need it, and review each tool action Claude proposes before it runs.
options.why: Trusted source, OAuth, per-conversation enablement and watching tool invocations are the help centre's own precautions for unverified custom connectors.

options.text: Enable the connector in every conversation for convenience and let actions run without review to save time.
options.why: Always-on tools and unreviewed actions maximise the blast radius if a tool result contains injected instructions.

options.text: Give Claude the consultant's ticketing-system password in the chat so it can log in directly.
options.why: Connectors use OAuth precisely so credentials are never shared in the conversation; pasting a password is a security failure.

explanation: Custom connectors reach arbitrary services not verified by Anthropic. Connect only to trusted organisations, authenticate via OAuth, enable tools per conversation, and monitor the actions Claude invokes, because malicious servers or tool content can attempt prompt injection.
reference: Claude Help Center — Getting started with custom integrations using remote MCP

stem: An operations team on an Enterprise plan uses the Gmail and Google Calendar connectors to triage vendor emails. Company policy requires a person to sign off every outbound vendor message, and it prohibits summarising emails that contain bank-account details into chats that might be shared. The Owner has allowed members to let connector actions run without asking. The team wants Claude to help reply to vendors faster. Which two practices keep the workflow inside policy? (Choose two.)

options.text: Turn on run-without-asking for send and reply actions so Claude can clear the queue during peak hours.
options.why: Removing the approval prompt removes the human sign-off the policy demands; the Owner allowing the option does not make using it compliant.

options.text: Export the whole vendor mailbox and upload it as project knowledge so Claude has everything in one place.
options.why: A mailbox dump puts bank details and other sensitive content into shared knowledge, the opposite of what the policy allows.

options.text: Keep the approval prompt for every send and reply so a team member reviews each outbound message before it goes.
options.why: Per-action approval is the built-in control that satisfies the sign-off requirement while Claude still does the drafting.

options.text: Rely on Claude to detect bank details in emails and refuse to summarise those automatically.
options.why: Detection by the model is probabilistic; it is a helpful hint but cannot be the policy control for regulated content.

options.text: Have Claude draft replies in the chat and flag emails that appear to contain payment details so the team handles those outside Claude, per policy.
options.why: Drafting speeds the work, and flagging likely payment emails for human handling routes the sensitive cases around the prohibited step instead of trusting the model to police it.

options.text: Connect a shared service account with broader mailbox access than individual members have, so Claude can see every thread.
options.why: Connectors are meant to inherit each person's own permissions; a broader shared credential bypasses access controls and accountability.

explanation: Connectors bring live data and actions, but organisational policy and permissions still govern their use. Keep human approval on actions the policy requires a person to sign off, and route sensitive content around Claude rather than relying on the model to catch it.
reference: Claude Help Center — Use Google Workspace connectors; Use connectors to extend Claude's capabilities

stem: A product manager is writing project instructions for a Project used to draft requirements. Which instruction text is most effective?

options.text: "Be smart, thorough and professional."
options.why: Vague adjectives give Claude nothing concrete to act on; every answer will interpret them differently.

options.text: "Never make mistakes and always produce correct, complete requirements."
options.why: Instructing Claude not to err does not reduce errors; it is an aspiration, not guidance about how to work.

options.text: A 1,500-word narrative covering the company's history, its products, its founders, its competitors and its market position, followed by the single line "use all of this context when writing requirements".
options.why: Background belongs in knowledge; long narrative instructions bury whatever behaviour the PM actually wants.

options.text: "You are a business analyst for a SaaS product team. Write requirements as user stories with Given/When/Then acceptance criteria. If information is missing, ask before assuming. Use plain English."
options.why: It names the role, the audience, the exact output format, the rule for gaps and the style, in a few sentences Claude can follow on every request.

explanation: Effective system-level instructions are short and specific: role, audience, output format, how to handle missing information, and style constraints. Adjectives, prohibitions on error and long background text do not shape behaviour.
reference: Claude Help Center — Understanding Claude's personalization features (project instructions)

stem: A marketing team's brand-voice Project has the instruction "Write in our brand voice." Drafts come out generic and interchangeable with any other company's copy. Which revision is most likely to fix this?

options.text: Describe the voice concretely: three tone attributes with a do and a don't each, two example sentences, banned words and the default format.
options.why: Concrete attributes, examples and banned words give Claude something to imitate and something to avoid, which is what "brand voice" was failing to convey.

options.text: Change the line to "YOU MUST ALWAYS write in our brand voice."
options.why: Emphasis does not add information; Claude still does not know what the voice is.

options.text: Paste the entire 40-page style guide into the instructions so that nothing about the voice is left out and Claude can consult every rule on every draft.
options.why: The style guide belongs in knowledge; dumping it into instructions makes them long and unfocused without distilling the rules that matter.

options.text: Repeat "brand voice" in the instructions and add a memory note asking Claude to remember it.
options.why: Repetition and memory do not define the voice; the missing ingredient is a specification, not a reminder.

explanation: Replace vague labels with explicit criteria: named attributes, do/don't pairs, short examples and banned terms. Emphasis, repetition and pasting whole guides do not make an instruction more specific.
reference: Claude Help Center — Understanding Claude's personalization features; Exam guide Domain 1 (clear prompts)

stem: An operations team is writing project instructions for a Project that classifies incoming vendor emails and drafts replies. Which two elements should the instructions contain? (Choose two.)

options.text: "Classify every email accurately."
options.why: An instruction to be accurate does not tell Claude what the categories mean or how to decide between them.

options.text: The exact category list with a one-line definition and an example for each, plus an "unsure" category that routes the email to a person.
options.why: Defined categories make classification consistent, and an explicit unsure route prevents forced guesses on ambiguous emails.

options.text: A table of every vendor's bank details so Claude can verify payment queries.
options.why: Bank details are sensitive data that the drafting task does not need; they do not belong in instructions or knowledge.

options.text: "If you are not sure which category applies, pick the most likely one and proceed."
options.why: Forcing a guess hides uncertainty from the team; ambiguous cases should be surfaced, not silently resolved.

options.text: The required output format: a table with category, one-line summary, suggested owner and a draft reply.
options.why: Specifying the output shape makes every response usable in the same way by every team member and easy to review.

options.text: "Send the reply through the Gmail connector as soon as the draft is ready."
options.why: Auto-sending removes the human review step; instructions should stop at the draft and leave sending to a person.

explanation: Good system-level instructions for a classification task define the categories with examples, provide an explicit route for uncertainty, and fix the output format. They do not include sensitive data, force guesses, or automate irreversible actions.
reference: Exam guide Domain 5 — Create effective system-level instructions; Domain 1 — effective prompts

stem: A consultant's engagement Project has the instruction "Always cite the statement-of-work section that supports each claim", and the SOW is in knowledge. When team members ask about topics the SOW does not cover, Claude cites section numbers that do not exist. Which change best fixes the instruction?

options.text: Add "Never hallucinate section numbers" to the instructions.
options.why: Telling Claude not to invent does not resolve the conflict it faces: it was told to always cite, even where nothing exists to cite.

options.text: Remove the citation requirement altogether.
options.why: Citations are valuable for in-scope claims; dropping them loses traceability to fix an edge case.

options.text: Change the instruction to cite the SOW section when one supports the claim, and when the SOW does not cover the topic, say so explicitly and give no citation; then test with several out-of-scope questions.
options.why: The failure is an instruction with no branch for the missing-information case; defining that branch and testing it removes the pressure to invent.

options.text: Upload more client documents so there is always something to cite.
options.why: More documents do not tell Claude what to do when a topic is uncovered, and they enlarge the knowledge without addressing the instruction defect.

explanation: An absolute instruction ("always cite") with no provision for the case where nothing applies pushes Claude to fabricate. Effective instructions say what to do when information is missing and are tested against those cases.
reference: Exam guide Domain 5 — effective system-level instructions; Domain 2 — hallucinations

stem: A school administrator's communications Project has 900 words of instructions that have grown over a year. In one chat she often needs both a parent letter and a staff briefing about the same event. Outputs have drifted: parent letters use staff jargon, and twice a draft included a student's name that a colleague had pasted in. She must keep student names out of all outputs, produce the right format for each audience, and be able to check quickly that a change worked. Which rewrite satisfies every requirement?

options.text: Split into two Projects, one for parent letters and one for staff briefings, each with a short instruction set.
options.why: Short instructions are right, but two Projects break the requirement to draft both audiences' documents about the same event in one chat.

options.text: Rewrite as a short, prioritised set: role and audiences; a format specification for each audience; a hard rule that outputs never include student names, with instructions to replace any name in the input with a placeholder and say so; and a saved set of test prompts to run after each edit.
options.why: It keeps both audiences in one Project, defines each format, handles the student-name case at the input as well as the output, and builds in the quick verification she needs.

options.text: Keep the 900 words but add "IMPORTANT: no student names, ever" in capitals at the top and bottom.
options.why: Emphasis on top of an already bloated instruction set does not fix the drift, and it says nothing about what to do when a name is pasted in.

options.text: Move all the rules into a knowledge file called `rules.md` so the instructions are empty and easy to maintain.
options.why: Rules in a knowledge file are reference material that may or may not be retrieved; standing constraints belong in instructions.

explanation: Long, accreted instructions drift. Rewrite them short and prioritised, with per-audience formats, an explicit rule for the sensitive-data case including how to handle it in inputs, and a test set to verify each change. Constraints that must always apply stay in instructions, not in knowledge.
reference: Claude Help Center — Understanding Claude's personalization features; Exam guide Domains 5 and 6

stem: A marketing team has published a new version of its brand guidelines with a new tagline. The brand-voice Project still contains last year's guidelines as knowledge. What should the Project maintainer do?

options.text: Replace the old file with the new guidelines, remove the superseded version, and test with a prompt that should use the new tagline.
options.why: Refreshing stale knowledge, removing the old version and testing the change is the basic maintenance loop that keeps a Project reliable.

options.text: Upload the new guidelines alongside the old ones so Claude has both for context.
options.why: Two versions of the same guide leave Claude to pick between them, and the old tagline will keep appearing.

options.text: Keep both files and add an instruction telling Claude to prefer the newer document whenever it finds a conflict between the two versions.
options.why: This keeps the stale file in play and relies on Claude noticing and resolving every conflict correctly.

options.text: Do nothing, since Claude will notice the tagline has changed from the team's prompts.
options.why: Claude does not update knowledge from usage; the old guidelines remain the reference until someone replaces them.

explanation: Keep knowledge current: when a source document is superseded, replace it, remove the old version, and run a quick test so the change is confirmed rather than assumed.
reference: Claude Help Center — How can I create and manage projects?

stem: An operations team's vendor-triage Project classifies emails into invoice, query, complaint and other. The business has started working with logistics carriers, and their emails now land in "other" every time, so nobody picks them up. What is the right maintenance action?

options.text: Tell each team member to mention the logistics category in their own prompts whenever they notice a carrier email, so the fix does not require touching the shared configuration.
options.why: Per-user workarounds are inconsistent and depend on people spotting the problem; the shared configuration is where the fix belongs.

options.text: Add a document about the carriers to project knowledge and leave the instructions unchanged.
options.why: Background knowledge does not change the category list Claude has been told to use; the classification rule itself needs updating.

options.text: Accept the behaviour, since Claude cannot be retrained on new categories.
options.why: No retraining is needed; categories are defined in the instructions and can be changed at any time.

options.text: Add a "logistics" category with a definition and example to the instructions, test on a few carrier emails, and tell the team.
options.why: Changing the instruction, testing it and communicating the change to the people using the Project is the complete maintenance cycle.

explanation: When the business changes, the configuration must follow: update the instruction that encodes the rule, test the change on real examples, and inform the users so everyone works from the same categories.
reference: Exam guide Domain 5 — Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions

stem: An HR team's onboarding Project has worked well for three months, but policies change several times a year and four people can edit the Project. Which maintenance routine best keeps the Project reliable over time?

options.text: Freeze the instructions and knowledge now, since they work, and avoid all changes.
options.why: Policies will change; a frozen Project drifts out of date and starts giving confidently wrong answers.

options.text: Name an owner, review knowledge quarterly and on each policy change, remove superseded files, keep a changelog, and rerun a fixed test set after every edit.
options.why: Ownership, scheduled review, removal of stale files, a changelog and a regression test set are the practices that keep a shared configuration trustworthy.

options.text: Let all four editors add any new document as soon as it appears, without removing anything, so nothing that might be relevant to a new hire's question is ever lost.
options.why: Uncoordinated additions with no removals accumulate contradictions and bloat, which degrades answers.

options.text: Rely on Claude's memory to track which policies have changed since the Project was created.
options.why: Memory holds conversational context about the user; it is not a mechanism for keeping knowledge files current.

explanation: Sustainable maintenance means an accountable owner, periodic and event-driven reviews, removal of superseded knowledge, a record of changes, and a regression set of test prompts to confirm each change.
reference: Exam guide Domain 5 — maintain and update configurations; Claude Help Center — How can I create and manage projects?

stem: A consultancy shares an engagement Project with six people on a Team plan, all with "Can edit". Yesterday someone changed the instructions and output quality dropped for everyone, but nobody knows what was changed or by whom. The team needs to recover quickly and stop this happening again. Which response best meets both needs?

options.text: Ask Claude in the Project to describe what changed in its instructions since last week.
options.why: Claude sees only the current instructions; it has no history of previous versions to compare against.

options.text: Delete the Project and rebuild it from memory, then share it again with everyone as editors.
options.why: Rebuilding from memory risks losing working details, and re-granting edit rights to all six recreates the conditions for the same problem.

options.text: Restore the last known good instructions from the copy kept outside the Project, reduce "Can edit" to two named maintainers with the others on "Can view", and require a changelog entry and a test run before any future edit.
options.why: A saved copy allows immediate recovery; narrowing edit rights and adding a change process prevent silent, untested edits in future.

options.text: Tell everyone to stop using the Project until the person who made the change comes forward.
options.why: This halts work without recovering anything and does nothing to prevent a repeat.

explanation: Shared configurations need version control outside the tool, limited edit permissions matched to roles, and a lightweight change process (log the change, run the tests). Claude cannot reconstruct its own configuration history.
reference: Claude Help Center — Manage project visibility and sharing (Can view / Can edit)

stem: A product team's requirements Project has degraded over four months: several new members joined, dozens of documents were added, and the default model changed. The team kept a 15-prompt test set with saved outputs from launch. Members propose several fixes, but the lead insists on diagnosing before changing anything. Which two actions should come first? (Choose two.)

options.text: Rerun the 15 launch prompts and compare each output with the saved baseline to see which behaviours changed.
options.why: The regression set is the fastest way to turn a vague sense of degradation into specific, observable differences.

options.text: Rewrite the instructions from scratch immediately, since they are probably the cause.
options.why: Rewriting before diagnosis may fix nothing and destroys the ability to attribute the change to a cause.

options.text: Switch to the most capable model tier and see whether quality recovers.
options.why: Changing the model is another uncontrolled variable; it does not identify what went wrong and may mask a knowledge problem.

options.text: Audit the knowledge files for duplicates, superseded versions and unrelated documents, and check the size of the instructions, before editing anything.
options.why: Accumulated stale or duplicate knowledge and instruction bloat are common causes of drift; auditing them shows what to remove or trim with evidence.

options.text: Add the team's recent Slack discussions as knowledge so Claude has the latest context.
options.why: Adding more unstructured content to an already bloated Project deepens the likely cause rather than diagnosing it.

options.text: Ask each new member to write their own instructions in their own chats to compensate.
options.why: Per-user workarounds fragment the shared configuration and make the degradation harder to diagnose.

explanation: Diagnose before changing: rerun the regression set against the baseline to see what changed, and audit knowledge and instructions for accumulated bloat. Only then make one change at a time and re-test.
reference: Exam guide Domains 5 and 7 — maintain configurations; diagnose and resolve issues
